title: Consistency and Consensus
summary: The strongest correctness guarantees for distributed systems and what they cost. Covers linearizability (single-object recency) and how it differs from serializability, causal ordering versus total ordering, total order broadcast, two-phase commit for atomic commit, and fault-tolerant consensus (Raft/Paxos/Zab) and the coordination services built on it.
keyTakeaways: Linearizability makes a system behave as if there is a single copy of the data with atomic operations: a recency guarantee on reads and writes of a single object.

Linearizability is NOT serializability: serializability is a transaction-isolation property over multiple objects (transactions equivalent to some serial order); combining both is 'strict serializability'.
The CAP theorem: under a network partition you must choose between linearizable (Consistent) and totally Available; and linearizability is often dropped for speed, not just availability.
Causal consistency preserves happens-before (a partial order) and is the strongest consistency achievable without slowing down under partitions; linearizability imposes a total order.
Total order broadcast (atomic broadcast) delivers messages reliably in the same order to all nodes and is equivalent to consensus and to linearizable compare-and-set.
Two-phase commit (2PC) is an atomic commit protocol with a coordinator; after a participant votes 'yes' it is in doubt and blocks holding locks if the coordinator crashes.

Fault-tolerant consensus (Paxos, Raft, Zab, VSR) provides uniform agreement, integrity, validity, and termination using epochs and quorums; FLP proves it is impossible in a purely asynchronous model but achievable with timeouts.

questions.q: In DDIA's precise definition, what does linearizability guarantee?
options: That a set of transactions is equivalent to executing them one at a time in some serial order
That the system behaves as if there were a single copy of the data, so once a read returns a new value every later read returns that value or newer (a recency guarantee on a single object)
That all replicas eventually converge to the same value given no new writes
That reads never block writes and writes never block reads
questions.explain: Linearizability (atomic/strong consistency) makes concurrent operations on a single object appear to take effect atomically at one instant, so the data looks like a single up-to-date copy: after any read observes a new value, all subsequent reads see it too. Option A is serializability, and option C describes mere eventual consistency.

questions.q: How does linearizability differ from serializability?
options: They are two names for the same guarantee
Serializability concerns a single object, while linearizability concerns whole transactions
Linearizability is a recency guarantee on reads/writes of a single object; serializability is an isolation guarantee that a set of multi-object transactions is equivalent to some serial order
Linearizability is weaker than eventual consistency, whereas serializability is stronger
questions.explain: Serializability is a transaction-isolation property: transactions (which may touch many objects) behave as if run one at a time in some serial order, but that order need not match real time. Linearizability is about the recency of individual object reads/writes in real-time order. A system providing both is called strictly serializable.

questions.q: Which of these genuinely requires linearizability to be correct?
options: Rendering a social-media timeline where slightly stale data is acceptable
Electing a single leader / acquiring a distributed lock, where two nodes must never both believe they hold it
Serving cached product images from the nearest region
Computing an approximate count of active users
questions.explain: Leader election and locking need linearizability: all nodes must agree on the single current holder, so a stale read could produce a dangerous split-brain. This is why coordination services like ZooKeeper/etcd provide linearizable operations. The other cases tolerate stale reads and do not need a recency guarantee.

questions.q: According to DDIA, what does the CAP theorem actually say?
options: A system can pick at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance at all times
Consistency and availability are always mutually exclusive regardless of partitions
Partitions never happen in a well-designed datacenter, so CAP is irrelevant
When a network partition occurs, a system must choose between being linearizable (Consistent) and being totally Available; when there is no partition it can be both
questions.explain: DDIA reframes CAP as: if the network is partitioned, you must sacrifice either linearizability or total availability; without a partition you can have both. The popular 'pick 2 of 3' phrasing is misleading because partition tolerance is not optional — partitions are a fact you must handle, not a property you choose. Note too that linearizability is often dropped for performance, not only availability.

questions.q: What is causal consistency, and what is its relationship to linearizability?
options: It preserves the happens-before (causal) partial order between operations, and is the strongest consistency model that does not slow down or become unavailable under network partitions
It enforces a single total order on all operations, making it stronger than linearizability
It is identical to eventual consistency but with vector clocks
It guarantees recency on single objects but not ordering between them
questions.explain: Causal consistency enforces only the partial order of causally related operations (happens-before), so concurrent operations may be seen in different orders on different nodes. Crucially it can remain available during partitions, making it the strongest consistency achievable without the coordination cost of linearizability, which instead imposes a full total order.

questions.q: Lamport timestamps provide a total order consistent with causality. Why are they nonetheless insufficient for something like enforcing a unique-username constraint?
options: Because Lamport timestamps can go backward, unlike wall clocks

Because the total order is only known in hindsight — a node cannot tell in the moment whether some other node is concurrently claiming the same name, so it needs total order broadcast to know when the order is finalized
Because Lamport timestamps require synchronized physical clocks to work
Because they only order operations on the same object, not across objects
questions.explain: Lamport timestamps define a total order, but to reject a duplicate username immediately a node must know it has seen all other claims — and it cannot, because a lower timestamp could still arrive later. You need the order finalized at the moment of the decision, which is what total order broadcast provides.

questions.q: What does total order broadcast (atomic broadcast) guarantee?
options: Messages are delivered to at least one node, in any order
Messages are delivered in causal order, but nodes may disagree on the order of concurrent messages
Messages are delivered in FIFO order per sender but not globally ordered
Messages are delivered reliably and in the exact same total order to every node
questions.explain: Total order broadcast requires two properties: reliable delivery (no message lost, all nodes get it) and totally ordered delivery (every node sees messages in the identical order). This is exactly what state-machine replication needs, and it turns out to be equivalent to consensus.

questions.q: In two-phase commit (2PC), what happens after a participant replies 'yes' in the prepare phase but the coordinator then crashes before sending the decision?
options: The participant unilaterally aborts and releases its locks after a short timeout
The participant commits automatically, since a 'yes' vote implies commit
The participant is 'in doubt' and must hold its locks and block until it can learn the coordinator's decision
The participant promotes itself to coordinator and decides for the whole cluster
questions.explain: Once a participant votes yes it has promised to commit if told to and can no longer decide on its own; the coordinator's write of the commit decision is the point of no return. If the coordinator crashes at that moment, the participant is stuck in doubt, holding locks and blocking, until the coordinator recovers — 2PC's central weakness.

questions.q: How is two-phase commit (2PC) related to, but distinct from, consensus algorithms like Paxos/Raft?
options: 2PC is an atomic commit protocol requiring all participants to vote yes and is blocking if the coordinator fails; consensus needs only a majority to agree and can tolerate node failures
2PC and consensus are the same protocol under different names
Consensus requires unanimity while 2PC needs only a majority
2PC tolerates coordinator failure automatically, whereas consensus blocks on a single failure
questions.explain: 2PC achieves atomic commit but requires every participant to agree and blocks if its single coordinator dies. Fault-tolerant consensus instead reaches agreement with only a majority (quorum) and survives minority failures, including of its leader. They are related — both about agreement — but 2PC is not fault-tolerant consensus.

questions.q: Which set of formal properties defines fault-tolerant consensus in DDIA?
options: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability
Uniform agreement, integrity, validity, and termination
Linearizability, causality, availability, and partition tolerance
Prepare, promise, accept, and learn
questions.explain: Consensus is defined by uniform agreement (no two nodes decide differently), integrity (a node decides at most once), validity (the decided value was proposed by some node), and termination (every non-crashed node eventually decides). Termination is the liveness property that FLP shows is impossible without timing assumptions. Option D lists the phases of Paxos, not the properties.

questions.q: What does the FLP impossibility result state about consensus?
options: Consensus is impossible whenever more than half the nodes fail
Consensus is impossible in the presence of Byzantine nodes
No deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus in a purely asynchronous system if even one node may crash — though consensus is achievable in practice using timeouts or randomization
Consensus always requires synchronized clocks with bounded drift
questions.explain: FLP proves that in a fully asynchronous model (no clocks, no timeouts) with even a single possible crash, no deterministic algorithm can always reach consensus, because you cannot tell a slow node from a dead one. Real systems escape this by adding partial-synchrony assumptions (timeouts) or randomization, so Raft and Paxos work fine in practice.

questions.q: Consensus is shown to be equivalent to several other problems. Which list is correct?
options: Total order broadcast, linearizable compare-and-set, and leader election
Two-phase commit, eventual consistency, and read repair
Snapshot isolation, causal consistency, and sloppy quorums
Vector clocks, anti-entropy, and hinted handoff
questions.explain: DDIA shows total order broadcast, a linearizable compare-and-set register, and leader election are all equivalent to consensus — solving any one lets you solve the others. The distractors mix in weaker mechanisms (eventual consistency, read repair, anti-entropy) that explicitly do not require consensus.

questions.q: How do consensus algorithms like Raft and Paxos use epoch (term/ballot) numbers together with quorums?
options: They give every node a fixed epoch at startup that never changes, avoiding elections
The epoch number is a wall-clock timestamp used to break ties between leaders
Quorums are only consulted for reads; writes go to the single leader without voting
Each election increments a monotonically increasing epoch number, and a leader must gather votes from a quorum; overlapping quorums guarantee any new leader learns of the latest committed decisions
questions.explain: Every leader election bumps a monotonically increasing epoch (term/ballot) number, and to act a leader needs votes from a quorum. Because two quorums always overlap in at least one node, any newly elected leader is guaranteed to have seen the most recent committed proposals, preventing two leaders with conflicting decisions from both succeeding.

questions.q: What core capabilities do coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd provide to applications?
options: High-throughput bulk data storage for application records
Linearizable atomic operations, total ordering of operations (e.g. via a monotonically increasing zxid), failure detection through ephemeral nodes/sessions, and change notifications (watches)
Column-oriented analytics with vectorized scans
Automatic sharding and rebalancing of the application's primary database
questions.explain: ZooKeeper/etcd expose a small set of consensus-backed primitives: linearizable atomic compare-and-set, a total order via a monotonically increasing transaction id, failure detection via ephemeral nodes tied to client sessions, and watches for change notifications. Applications use these for leader election, locks, service discovery, and membership — not for storing large volumes of application data.
